sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial Keratitis (MK) is an infectious process involving the corneal epithelium and stroma. A 'corneal abscess' specifically refers to a localized collection of white blood cells (neutrophils), necrotic tissue, and pathogens within the stroma, often presenting as a dense, yellowish-white opacity with an overlying epithelial defect.

rows: Chronic lid disease, post-op, bullous keratopathy.
Rapidly spreading, soup-like melting, greenish discharge.
Serpiginous ulcer, deep stromal abscess, hypopyon.
Indolent, often in the inferior cornea.
Feathery margins, satellite lesions, immune ring.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Pathogenesis
content: 1. Stage of Infiltration: PMN migration from limbus/tears into the stroma.
2. Stage of Active Ulceration: Necrosis and sloughing of epithelium and stroma.
3. Stage of Regression: Immune response limits the infection; lines of demarcation form.
4. Stage of Cicatrization: Healing via fibroblast activity, resulting in permanent nebula, macula, or leucoma.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags for Perforation
content: Descemetocele formation (clear bubble in the floor of the ulcer)
Sudden decrease in IOP (intraocular pressure)
Seidel's test positive (aqueous leak)
Shallow or flat anterior chamber
Iris prolapse into the corneal defect
Rapidly progressive stromal thinning ('melting')

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: The Scrape Protocol
content: 1. Stop antibiotics 24-48h if possible (unless severe).
2. Instill topical anesthetic (Proparacaine preferred over Tetracaine).
3. Scrape the base and the active margins using a Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
4. Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, and Sabouraud Dextrose Agar.
5. Prepare slides for Gram and Giemsa stains (and KOH/Calcofluor white if fungal suspected).

sections.title: Initial Management: Medical Protocol
content: Monotherapy (Non-central, <2mm): Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5% or Gatifloxacin 0.5%) q1h.
Duotherapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/mL) + Fortified Vancomycin (50mg/mL) q1h around the clock.
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% BID or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce pain and prevent synechiae.
Oral Doxycycline: 100mg BID to inhibit collagenase and prevent melting.
Steroid Timing: Wait at least 48-72h of effective antibiotic cover (SCUT trial recommendations).

sections.title: Fortified Antibiotic Preparation (Pearls)
sections.content: Vancomycin (50mg/mL): Add 10mL of sterile water or BSS to 500mg Vancomycin powder. Stable for 14 days refrigerated. Tobramycin (15mg/mL): Add 2mL of injectable Tobramycin (40mg/mL) to a 5mL bottle of 0.3% Tobramycin ophthalmic solution.

content.explanation: P: Painful (Severe), S: Soup-like melt, E: Extended wear CL risk, U: Ulceration rapid, D: Discharge (Greenish/Purulent), O: Odor (often associated with Pseudomonas cultures).

branches: Amniotic Membrane Graft (for persistent epithelial defects)
Bandage Contact Lens (only after infection is sterilized)

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SCUT Trial
content: Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT).
Finding: No significant difference in visual outcome at 3 months for the whole group.
Subgroup benefit: Patients with very poor baseline vision and central/deep ulcers showed better outcomes with early steroids (after 48h of antibiotics).
Key Rule: Never start steroids until the organism is identified and fungal/acanthamoeba are ruled out.

sections.title: Complications and Prognosis
content: Endophthalmitis (Infection spread to the vitreous/aqueous).
Secondary Glaucoma (Inflammatory debris blocking the trabecular meshwork).
Anterior Polychromatic Cataract.
Corneal Leucoma (Permanent opaque scar).
Phthisis Bulbi (Shrinkage of the eye following severe infection).

sections.title: Pathogens that can Penetrate Intact Epithelium

content.explanation: N: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, H: Haemophilus influenzae, L: Listeria monocytogenes, C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Lid Flip': Always evert the eyelid to look for retained foreign bodies (e.g., a lost contact lens) which can be the nidus for infection.
Acanthamoeba Hint: Pain out of proportion to clinical signs and radial keratoneuritis.
Moraxella: Classically occurs in patients with pre-existing ocular surface disease and malnutrition.
Toxicity vs. Infection: If the ulcer is not improving, consider if the 1-hour drops are causing 'medicamentosa' or toxic epithelial toxicity.
Hypopyon: In bacterial ulcers, the hypopyon is usually sterile (inflammatory); in fungal ulcers, it may contain active fungal elements.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Microbial Keratitis: The Suppurative Storm ---
sections.content: Bacterial keratitis is a sight-threatening ocular emergency characterized by rapid corneal destruction and stromal suppuration. Management requires immediate identification of risk factors, grading of severity, and aggressive, broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy to prevent perforation and permanent scarring.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Microbial (bacterial) keratitis is a serious infection of the corneal stroma. Unlike viral or sterile keratitis, it often presents with an epithelial defect overlying a dense, necrotic stromal infiltrate, often accompanied by significant anterior chamber inflammation (hypopyon). Most bacteria (except N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis, C. diphtheriae, and H. influenzae) require a breach in the corneal epithelium to initiate infection.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cascade of Destruction
content: 1. Epithelial Breach: Trauma or contact lens-induced hypoxia creates an entry point.
2. Adherence: Bacteria utilize fimbriae or pili to bind to the exposed corneal stroma/extracellular matrix.
3. Invasion & Multiplication: Organisms replicate and release exotoxins (e.g., Exotoxin A in Pseudomonas).
4. Host Response: Neutrophil infiltration (chemotaxis) releases matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
5. Stromal Melting: Combination of bacterial toxins and host enzymes leads to keratomalacia (liquefactive necrosis).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Scraping Protocol
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia: Proparacaine is preferred (Benoxinate may be more bacteriostatic).
2. Sample Collection: Use a Kimura spatula, 25G needle, or sterile blade to scrape the leading edge and base.
3. C-Streaks: Transfer directly to agar plates using 'C-streaks' for semi-quantitative assessment.
4. Slide Prep: Gram and Giemsa/Diff-Quik stains for immediate visualization.
5. Culture: Blood Agar (aerobes), Chocolate Agar (fastidious), Sabouraud (fungi), Thioglycollate (anaerobes).

sections.title: Primary Medical Management
content: Loading Dose: 1 drop every 5–15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30–60 minutes around the clock.
Monotherapy (Mild/Mod): 4th Generation Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin 0.5%, Gatifloxacin 0.5%, Besifloxacin 0.6%).
Duo-therapy (Severe/Central): Fortified Tobramycin (14 mg/mL) AND Fortified Vancomycin (25-50 mg/mL).
Cycloplegia: Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1% TID to reduce ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae.
Systemic Rx: Consider if scleral involvement (e.g., Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID) or N. gonorrhoeae (Ceftriaxone 1g IM/IV).

sections.title: Steroid Use: The SCUT Trial (2011)
sections.content: The Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT) found no significant difference in 3-month visual outcomes between topical corticosteroids and placebo. However, a subgroup analysis showed benefit in vision for central, deep, and severe ulcers (excluding Nocardia). RULE: Start steroids only AFTER 48-72 hours of clinical improvement and negative cultures, and NEVER if fungus or Acanthamoeba is suspected.

branches: Marginal Keratitis (Sterile, lucid interval at limbus)

sections.title: CRITICAL: Red Flags for Worsening
content: Enlarging Infiltrate or Epithelial Defect despite 48h therapy.
Progressive Stromal Thinning (Descemetocele or Perforation).
Scleral involvement (Scleritis/Scleral melting).
Rise in Intraocular Pressure (Secondary Glaucoma).
Signs of Endophthalmitis (hypopyon increase, vitreous cells, loss of red reflex).

content.explanation: P: Pain (is it increasing?); E: Epithelial defect size; D: Discharge (purulent?); A: Anterior chamber reaction/hypopyon; L: Location and Size of infiltrate.

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<2mm) or impending perforation.
Tectonic Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): For large perforations or uncontrolled infection.
Amniotic Membrane Graft (AMG): Promotes re-epithelialization in neurotrophic cases.
PACK-CXL: Photoactivated Chromophore for Keratitis (Cross-linking) as adjuvant therapy for resistant organisms.

rows: Enriched with Factor V and X
Low pH, contains antibiotics to inhibit bacteria

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: Contact lens wearers with ulcers have Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.
Wessely Ring: An immune ring (antigen-antibody complex) often seen in Gram-negative infections.
Fortified drops are generally stable for 7-14 days if refrigerated.
Never use a 'taper' on antibiotics until the infection is sterilized; maintain 'therapeutic' levels.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Corneal Scarring/Leucoma (Permanent vision loss if central).
Irregular Astigmatism (Secondary to scarring).
Anterior Synechiae and Secondary Glaucoma.
Infectious Endophthalmitis (Rare unless perforation occurs).
Phthisis Bulbi (In severe, untreated cases).

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Microbial Keratitis: The Sight-Threatening Emergency ---
sections.content: An urgent, sight-threatening infection of the corneal stroma characterized by epithelial defect, infiltrate, and associated inflammation. Rapid diagnosis and targeted antimicrobial therapy are mandatory to prevent stromal melting and permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: Microbial keratitis is an infection involving the corneal stroma, often secondary to contact lens wear, ocular surface disease, or trauma. Globally, bacterial keratitis is the most common form, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa being the most frequent pathogen in contact lens wearers. Incidence is estimated at 2.5–799 per 100,000 person-years depending on geography and risk factor prevalence.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Intervention Required
content: Corneal thinning or impending perforation (Seidel positive)
Involvement of the visual axis (central location)
Hypopyon exceeding 2mm
Scleral involvement (Sclerokeratitis)
Lack of response to initial therapy at 24-48 hours

rows: Peripheral, smaller, less pain, no hypopyon
Radial perineuritis, severe pain out of proportion to exam
Feathery edges, satellite lesions, slow progression

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity & Slit-lamp exam (map infiltrate size).
Step 2: Corneal scrapings using Kimura spatula or platinum blade.
Step 3: Inoculate onto Blood Agar, Chocolate Agar, Sabouraud Agar, and Thioglycolate broth.
Step 4: Perform Gram stain and initiate empiric fortified antibiotics.
Step 5: Perform in-vivo confocal microscopy if Acanthamoeba/Fungal suspected.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol: Fortified Antibiotics
content: Fortified Tobramycin (15mg/ml) q1h
Fortified Cefazolin (50mg/ml) q1h
Monotherapy: Gatifloxacin or Moxifloxacin 0.5% (for smaller lesions)
Cycloplegics (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%) for pain
Topical steroids: Only after epithelialization and reduced organism load

content.explanation: S: Staining (Fluorescein), T: Tincture (Stains like Gram), A: Acanthamoeba check, M: Microscopy (Confocal), P: Pathogen identification

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for contact lens case contamination.
Avoid eye patching; it creates a warm, hypoxic environment for bacterial growth.
The 'SCUT trial' provided evidence that adjunctive topical corticosteroids do not improve visual outcomes at 3 months for bacterial ulcers.
If the patient is monocular, hospitalize for intensive monitoring.
